name: Dowager's hump correction

card.summary: Exercise, posture work and clinical care aimed at reducing an exaggerated upper-back curve (hyperkyphosis), giving a more upright torso, a neck that sits over the shoulders and a taller-looking frame.
card.note: A pronounced curve can reflect osteoporotic vertebral fractures or another spinal condition, which clinicians evaluate separately from posture.

quick.overview:
Dowager's hump is the popular name for an exaggerated forward curve of the upper (thoracic) spine, clinically called hyperkyphosis. It is usually defined as a curve above about 40 to 45 degrees, and it shows up as rounded upper back, forward head position and a shorter-looking torso. Correcting or reducing it is pursued to look more upright, taller and more open through the chest and shoulders.

Postural kyphosis is the most common type and is generally approached with posture re-education and strengthening. Small trials have examined yoga and McKenzie-style exercise programs in affected women, and chiropractic and physiotherapy case reports describe improvement. Severe or structural curves, including those from vertebral fractures, are managed medically and occasionally surgically.
quick.how: People work on it with upper-back and scapular strengthening, chest and neck mobility work, posture habits during desk and phone use, yoga, and sometimes physiotherapy or chiropractic care. Results are gradual and depend on whether the curve is postural (flexible) or structural.
quick.risks: A visible curve in an older adult can be a sign of vertebral compression fractures from osteoporosis, so clinicians recommend medical assessment, including bone density, when the curve is pronounced or painful. Surgery for severe deformity carries reported complication and reoperation rates, and its cosmetic effect is not always stable.

lead: Dowager's hump is the colloquial term for hyperkyphosis, an exaggerated forward rounding of the upper back. A normal thoracic curve is roughly 20 to 45 degrees; beyond about 40 to 45 degrees it is described as hyperkyphosis [3][4]. In looksmaxxing and posture circles, correcting it is pursued because a flatter upper back lets the head sit over the shoulders, opens the chest and increases standing height and frame presence.

Most cases in younger people are postural, linked to slouching, and are generally approached with posture re-education and strengthening exercises [3]. In older women the same appearance is classically associated with osteoporosis and vertebral compression fractures [5].

Research on correction is small. A pilot trial of yoga in women with hyperkyphosis, trials of McKenzie exercise for neck disability in women with a hump and individual case reports are the main human studies; none establishes a standard protocol [1][6][7].

chain: Strengthen and mobilize the upper back
Reduce thoracic rounding and forward head position
More upright torso, neck over shoulders
angle.text: Reducing thoracic rounding changes how the head, neck and shoulders stack, which people use to look taller and more upright. How much a curve can change depends on whether it is postural or structural.

paras: Kyphosis is the forward convex curvature of the spine. The thoracic spine is naturally kyphotic; a measurement above roughly 40 degrees (a threshold used in yoga research as the 95th percentile of young adults) or 45 degrees is labelled hyperkyphosis, popularly 'dowager's hump' [3][4]. The term carries a long association with older, postmenopausal women with osteoporosis [5][8].

Causes listed in clinical references include habitual slouching (postural kyphosis, the most common), Scheuermann's kyphosis from wedged vertebrae developing in adolescence, congenital malformations, nutritional deficiency, tuberculosis-related deformity, trauma and osteoporotic fractures [3]. One survey of 20- to 64-year-old women found kyphosis in about 35 percent of a healthy sample, and in postmenopausal women the measure correlated inversely with age [2]. A review has proposed that muscle ageing and strength may play a role in kyphosis and merits further study [1].

Postural kyphosis can often be treated with posture re-education and strengthening exercises, which also ease strain on overstretched back muscles [3]. In growing children with structural curves, bracing has produced lasting improvement; in postmenopausal osteoporosis one randomized trial reported benefit from body braces, and techniques such as the Schroth method are used in some countries [3].

Severe curves may be treated surgically. Kyphoplasty is used for progressive deformity from vertebral collapse, and spinal fusion for high-degree curves. A review of surgical studies reports serious complication risk around 5 percent and reoperation in about 5 percent within five years, and notes that the cosmetic result is not necessarily stable [3].

The upper-back curve is discussed in posture-focused parts of appearance culture, where a rounded upper back and forward head are described as making a person look shorter and less broad. Correction is framed as a free-standing improvement alongside neck posture and shoulder width work. Practitioners typically combine upper-back strengthening, mobility work and attention to desk and phone posture.

A single-arm pilot trial in women with hyperkyphosis tested a yoga program and measured anthropometric and physical-function outcomes [6]. A trial of 30 women with a cervical dowager's hump examined McKenzie exercises on functional neck disability, and a later study compared McKenzie and Kendall exercises [7]. A 2023 case report described a 61-year-old woman whose symptoms and spinal alignment improved over nine months of chiropractic care with home stretching [8]. A 1993 survey measured kyphosis prevalence in healthy women [2]. These are small and varied designs; no large randomized trial of cosmetic correction is cited.

Clinical sources note that a pronounced curve in an older adult may reflect vertebral fractures, and about one-third of the most severe hyperkyphosis cases in older people involve them [3]. Bone-density evaluation is part of diagnosis [3]. Surgical options carry the complication rates noted above [3].

lore.intro: Posture-oriented communities describe upper-back rounding as a correctable look flaw, usually through training and habit change.

claims.claim: Strengthening and mobility work can reduce upper-back rounding and improve how upright someone looks
claims.believers: Practitioners say exercise and posture habits reduce a rounded upper back and forward head over months, producing a taller, more open appearance.
claims.experts: Clinical references say postural kyphosis can often be treated with posture re-education and strengthening [3]; a yoga pilot trial and McKenzie exercise studies examined women with hyperkyphosis [6][7].

claims.claim: Manual or chiropractic correction can resolve a dowager's hump
claims.believers: Chiropractic proponents cite cases where alignment and symptoms improved with spinal manipulation.
claims.experts: A 2023 single case report described improvement in a 61-year-old woman after nine months of care [8]; no controlled trial is cited.
